title: Introspection: help(), id(), dir()
reflection_prompt: Of help(), id(), and dir(), which do you think you'll actually reach for while coding on your own? Why?

exercises.title: Asking Python for Help
description: Call help(len), with no other output.
<pre>> python program.py
Help on built-in function len in module builtins:
len(obj, /)
Return the number of items in a container.
help() prints a function's built-in documentation
— its name, what arguments it takes, and what it does —
without you needing to look anything up online. This is usually the
fastest way to answer "wait, what does this function actually do?"
while you're coding.
Since the exact wording Python prints can change slightly between
versions, this exercise (and the rest of this unit's
help() exercises) only checks that certain key pieces of
text show up somewhere in the output — not that it matches
character-for-character.

exercises.title: help() on a Method
description: Call help(str.upper).
<pre>> python program.py
Help on method_descriptor:
upper(self, /)
Return a copy of the string converted to uppercase.
help() isn't just for standalone functions like
len() — it works on methods too, like the
.upper() string method you used back in the strings
unit. Notice the syntax: str.upper, not
"hello".upper — you're asking about the method
itself, not calling it on a particular string.

exercises.title: Using help() to Discover an Argument
description: The built-in sorted() function has a keyword argument
that reverses the sort order — but this unit isn't going to
tell you its name. Call help(sorted) first to find it,
then use sorted() with that argument to print the list
[3, 1, 4, 1, 5] sorted from
largest to smallest.
<pre>> python program.py
This is the real-world way help() gets used: not to
read documentation for its own sake, but to answer a specific
question — "does this function have an option for what I'm
trying to do?" — right when you need the answer.

exercises.title: Listing What a String Can Do
description: Read a string, then print whether "upper" appears in
dir() of that string.
<pre>> python program.py
hello
True
dir(value) returns a list of every attribute and
method a value has — for a string, that includes things like
.upper(), .split(), and .strip(),
all methods you've already used. Rather than printing the whole
(long) list, this checks for one specific name using
in, the same way you checked for a key in a
dictionary.
starter: # TODO: print whether "upper" is in dir(s)

exercises.title: Checking What a Tuple Can't Do
description: Print whether "sort" appears in dir(())
— that is, in the list of things an empty tuple
supports.
<pre>> python program.py
False
Tuples don't have a .sort() method at all, since
sorting would mean changing the tuple in place — and tuples
are immutable. dir() is a quick way to check whether a
type supports something before you try it and get an
error, instead of guessing.
starter: # TODO: print whether "sort" is in dir(())

exercises.title: Same Object, Same id()
description: Create a list a = [1, 2, 3], then set
b = a — not a new list, just another name for the
same one. Print whether id(a) equals id(b).
<pre>> python program.py
True
Every value in Python has an id() — a number
that uniquely identifies it in memory while your program runs. Since
id() is different every time a program runs, this
exercise (like the rest of this unit's id() exercises)
checks whether two ids are equal to each other,
rather than checking any specific id value.
Because b was assigned directly from a,
they refer to the exact same list in memory — so their ids
match.
starter: # TODO: print whether id(a) equals id(b)

exercises.title: Equal Value, Different id()
description: Create two separate lists that happen to contain
the same values: a = [1, 2, 3] and
c = [1, 2, 3]. Print whether id(a) equals
id(c).
<pre>> python program.py
False
Even though a and c look identical when
printed, and a == c would say True, they're
two separate list objects sitting in two separate places in memory
— so their ids are different. This is the difference between
two things being equal and two things being
the same object.
starter: # TODO: print whether id(a) equals id(c)

exercises.title: Find the Method, Then Use It
description: Read a string. Use dir() to confirm that strings have
a method for counting how many times a character or substring
appears (its name starts with c), then use that method
to print how many times the letter "l" appears in the
string.
<pre>> python program.py
hello world
3
This is the combined skill this unit is really building:
when you're not sure a type has the method you need, check
dir() first, then look up how to use it with
help() if the name alone isn't enough — instead of
guessing, or assuming it doesn't exist.
